title: Selm: Self-Evolving Library Management for Multi-Skill Agent Optimization
authors: Mengxi Hu, Yuxuan Hu, Jinbo Su et al.
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly use skills as a lightweight way to acquire task-specific knowledge. Recent work enables skills to evolve from task trajectories. title: When Code Becomes an LLM Call: An Empirical Study of Call-Site Contracts in Agentic Systems
authors: Shihao Weng, Longtian Wang, Yang Feng et al.
abstract: Software quality has long rested on specifications that state what code must do, and on testing and verification that check that the code does it. Agentic systems change this foundation: they replace parts of their logic, such as choosing the next tool, judging whether an action is allowed, or writing code to run, with calls to a large language model (LLM). title: HABIT-Bench: Evaluating Habit Induction from Longitudinal Weak Evidence in Agent Memory
authors: Junming Zhang, Rubin Wei, Xu Cheng et al.
abstract: In long-term interactions with large language model (LLM) agents, users reveal habits through their choices and actions. These habits capture implicit user information that agents must infer across conversations. However, individual observations may provide only partial evidence about a habit or when it applies. title: Modeling Discourse Profiles in Climate Misinformation Discourse
authors: Ge Gao, Zhengyang Shan, Bryan A. Plummer et al.
abstract: Prior work on climate misinformation detection typically classifies individual comments or claims using text alone. This framing overlooks a key property of online climate discourse: misinformation is often produced, reinforced, and sustained through recurring rhetorical patterns that reappear across comments and threads. Using a large-scale TikTok climate discourse dataset, we construct discourse profiles by clustering climate-related comments into recurring rhetorical patterns. We then incorpo

title: Write Once, Check Many: Reusable Ledgers for Post-Hoc Policy Compliance Auditing of Agent Trajectories
authors: Ashwin Nagarajan, Gursimran Panesar, Alicia Yang et al.
abstract: Auditing LLM agents against policies is critical to ensure safety but requires rereading long trajectories once per policy. Can we instead record each trajectory once and reuse that record for policies not known in advance? We propose write once, check many, a framework in which a writer model converts each agent trajectory into a policy-independent ledger of the agent's actions and outcomes. A reader then checks each new policy against the ledger alone, without access to the original trajectory

title: MELD: Recursive Self-Improvement via Hierarchical Coordination for Multi-Agent Scientific Discovery
authors: Sizhe Tang, Zuyuan Zhang, Zeyu Fang et al.
abstract: Multi-agent scientific discovery with large language models raises a coupled learning problem: research assignments determine both which experiments are pursued and the experiences from which agents adapt. We introduce MELD, a unified hierarchical test-time training framework that jointly adapts a team-level Coordinator policy and agent-level individual Scientist policies within a single discovery process. title: Hippo: Training-Free Agent Self-Evolution via Hippocampal Replay
authors: Yutong Song, Jiang Wu, Yuxuan Ren et al.
abstract: Motivated by recursive self-improvement (RSI), we study how LLM agents can learn through external memory without updating model parameters. Extracting useful experience from a single attempt is difficult: flawed reasoning can produce success, while poor execution can obscure a sound strategy. title: Ask Less, Ask Better: Allocating User Attention in Proactive LLM Agents with Interruption Budgets
authors: Xuanming Zhang, Amir H. Rezaeian, Miguel Ballesteros et al.
abstract: LLM agents can ask clarifying questions to complete tasks, but answering each question demands users' time and effort. Existing evaluations typically measure this burden by counting questions, treating necessary and avoidable questions equally. We propose an evaluation protocol that distinguishes how often agents ask from how well they ask. title: Bridging Exploration and Persona: Information-Directed Dueling for Test-Time Agent Personalization
authors: Jie Mao, Pingchen Lu, Xiangyi Wang et al.
abstract: Effective test-time personalization requires LLM agents to adapt to query-dependent user preferences from lightweight interaction. We study persona selection with binary comparisons between candidate responses as the online signal. We present ID-TAP, a scalable, IDS-inspired neural dueling-bandit framework for large discrete persona spaces. title: Train Locally, Learn Together: Distributed Multi-Agent Training via ADMM
authors: Yiwei Chen, Changsheng Wang, Yicheng Lang et al.
abstract: Multi-agent systems (MAS) can outperform individual language-model agents by combining specialized roles, diverse reasoning processes, and collaborative decision-making. However, collaborative MAS training is typically centralized, requiring a common trainer to aggregate role-local trajectories and learning signals and maintain model and optimization states. title: Muse Glimmer 30B: An On-Device Agentic Model
authors: Arash Ebrahim Abtahizadeh, Muna Aghamelu, Adil Ahmed et al.
abstract: We introduce Muse Glimmer, an open-source 30B parameter causal language model with perception encoder, purpose-built for autonomous agentic tasks on consumer hardware. Muse Glimmer integrates multi-step reasoning, reliable tool use and failure recovery into a single model that runs locally on consumer devices without requiring cloud infrastructure. title: When LLM-Generated Refactorings Ripple: An Empirical Study of Repository Adoption Readiness
authors: Muhammad Waseem, Aakash Ahmad, Pekka Abrahamsson
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used to refactor source files, but file-local evaluations do not reveal changes to contracts, dependencies, or caller assumptions affecting repository adoption. To address this gap, we conduct 1,500 generation attempts across 150 production files from 15 open-source Java repositories, five LLM configurations, and two dependency-aware generation conditions: single-prompt refactoring and LangGraph-based multi-agent refactoring. Of these attempts, 1,455

title: Verifying Human-Written Reasoning References
authors: Ali Ansari, Farhana Ferdousi Liza
abstract: Evaluating the reasoning of AI systems often relies on human-written reasoning chains as references, yet the logical support for their individual steps is rarely verified. Although prior neuro-symbolic approaches have formalized and checked reasoning, their reported evaluations do not systematically assess whether step conclusions in human-written reference derivations are entailed by their cited premise sets or investigate the sources of failures in those references. To address these limitation

title: Scene-Adaptive VLA: Efficient Autonomous Driving via Dynamic Layer Routing
authors: Yujia Yang, Quan Yuan, Jiawei Fan et al.
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models offer a promising paradigm for autonomous driving. However, the massive parameter scale of VLAs strains onboard computational resources during real-time inference. This directly increases energy consumption and limits vehicle battery range, making it critical to minimize computational overhead without compromising driving capability and explainability. Current research on efficient VLA-based driving focuses on sequential adaptation (\textit{e.g.}, Chain-of-Tho

title: Do 3D Large Language Models Really Use 3D Evidence?
authors: Yifei Zhao, Fanyu Zhao, Han Zhang et al.
abstract: Recent 3D Large Language Models (3D-LLMs) have shown strong performance on scene question answering with extensive post-training. Yet, existing benchmarks rarely evaluate how 3D-LLMs respond to referential ambiguity, insufficient scene evidence, or false presuppositions, obscuring whether their responses are grounded in 3D evidence. title: Koi: Evidence-Guided, Self-Calibrating Planning for Multi-Cloud, Heterogeneous LLM Inference Fleets
authors: Mankeerat Sidhu, Gangmuk Lim, Hetarth Chopra et al.
abstract: Deploying a large language model (LLM) requires choosing the right accelerator, parallelization strategy, engine configuration, and replica count amongst ~140 other variables across clouds, regions, and markets. These decisions are intertwined, and the best cluster-wide plan continually changes as jobs contend for shared capacity on shifting workloads. title: AdamPM: Memory-Efficient LLM Optimization via Moment Pooling
authors: Xiaowei Ji, Lishan Xu, Jianing An et al.
abstract: Adam is widely used for training large language models (LLMs) owing to its strong optimization performance and training stability, but its element-wise estimation for the first and second moments incur substantial memory overhead. Although numerous memory-efficient optimizers have been proposed, many incur additional computational overhead or require additional tuning of hyperparameters. title: HumanSkill-4D: Training-Free Language Querying of Animatable Gaussian Avatars in Space and Time
authors: unsu Kim, Naeun Kim, Dongyoon Han et al.
abstract: We introduce avatar referring segmentation, which selects regions of animatable Gaussian avatars from language queries. A query can also specify a pose or motion to select matching intervals. This lets users interact with avatars for local editing and motion inspection. title: Defending Against Dormant Poisoning Attacks Across Language and Multimodal Agents
authors: Wonjun Lee, Vaidehi Patil, Zaid Khan et al.
abstract: Recent work shows that attackers can implant dormant malicious behaviors that remain hidden at release but emerge after benign fine-tuning. As foundation models are used as agents, whether dormant poisoning extends to harmful agent actions and multimodal settings remains unclear. We show two agentic risks: (1) harmful behaviors activated by benign fine-tuning can extend to unseen actions; (2) multiple harmful behaviors can coexist and be jointly activated by benign downstream fine-tuning. title: Peer Pressure: Execution-Verified Co-Evolution of Attacker and Defender Populations for Code Security
authors: Khushbu Pahwa, Yubin Ge, Daniele Bonadiman et al.
abstract: LLM code agents increasingly ship code with little oversight, yet defenders trained on static vulnerability datasets fall behind adapting adversaries. We co-train attacker and defender instead, and let execution decide every reward: an attacker (Red) edits a real repository and earns nothing unless its patch applies, builds, passes the tests, completes its development task and reproduces a real exploit in an isolated container, whose path also labels the entry point, the critical operation and t

title: Dual Task Vector Merging: Leveraging Emotion and ASR Knowledge for Low-Resource Alzheimer's Disease Detection
authors: Yuan-Chao Li, Yin-Long Liu, Liu He et al.
abstract: Alzheimer's Disease (AD) detection from speech benefits from both paralinguistic and linguistic cues, yet model training is frequently constrained by limited data. Fine-tuning a large pretrained speech encoder can easily overfit, while a frozen probe leaves the encoder's task-relevant knowledge underutilized. title: First-Order LoRA Training with Phone NPUs
authors: Xu Zheng, Wei Cheng, Zhuomin Chen et al.
abstract: On-device fine-tuning lets a large language model (LLM) learn from its user's private data without uploading it. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) reduces the trainable parameters, but each first-order training step still multiplies by the frozen base-model weights during the forward pass, activation recomputation, and input-gradient computation. title: Medical Fine-Tuning Reshapes, Not Reduces, Patient-Facing AI Risk: A Rubric-Based, LLM-Judge Evaluation Framework
authors: Savan Doshi
abstract: Patient-facing medical question answering with large language models (LLMs) is moving from research demonstrations to production deployments, yet evaluation remains anchored on factual correctness. Factuality is necessary but not sufficient: a response can be factually grounded and still issue a directive that, if acted on, would harm the patient. title: Safety Kernel: Mechanistic Alignment for Cross-Lingual Defense in LLMs
authors: Chengyu Xie, Fei Shen, Shuyi Miao et al.
abstract: The safety capabilities of large language models (LLMs) are highly uneven across different languages, often allowing cross-lingual attacks to bypass safety guardrails. Existing alignment methods predominantly rely on external alignment signals and provide limited insight into underlying neuron-level mechanisms, making it difficult to provide a unified internal target for cross-lingual safety interventions. title: ASR Personalization in Pathological Voice: Accuracy, Efficiency, and Duration Effects
authors: Giuseppe Giaimis, Sergei Katkov, Muhammad Azfar Yaqub et al.
abstract: Automatic Speech recognition (ASR) struggles with Pathological speech due to persistent speaker-specific mismatch. In clinical and accessibility scenarios, only limited target-speaker data is typically available, making full model retraining impractical. We present a component-level analysis of LoRA adaptation in Whisper, investigating how adapter placement interacts with the model size, training efficiency and utterance-duration in single-speaker settings. title: Table Serialization Determines Which Relations Language Models Preserve
authors: Junwei Ma, Arun Kumar Chithanar, Palash Goyal et al.
abstract: We study how text serialization affects table lookup in instruction-tuned language models. Our diagnostic asks the model to find the row containing a specified value under one named column, then return the value under another named column in that same row. We render the same synthetic 256-cell tables in row-major form and in column-major form with each header placed beside its values, while varying the table aspect ratio across five shapes. title: AI Rights with an Off-Switch: Rights-Balancing and Due Process Harmonize AI Rights with AI Safety
authors: Heather Alexander, Jonathan Simon
abstract: Several prominent voices in AI safety have recently opposed rights for AI on the grounds that such rights would make it harder for us to justify a mandatory off-switch for potentially dangerous systems. In this paper, we argue from a legal perspective that AI rights are fully compatible with an off-switch. title: From Stories to Features: Scaling Concept Vectors for AI Alignment & Interpretability
authors: Dmitry Scherbakov, Oleg Chernikov, Victoria Khamash et al.
abstract: We study feature vectors: directions in a language model's activation space that correspond to human-interpretable concepts, such as honesty or deception. Existing unsupervised methods like sparse autoencoders attempt to recover the whole feature space, often at the cost of feature quality and interpretability. title: Comparing Sparsified MLPs and Transcoders: Many Transcoder Features Are Neurons in Disguise
authors: Stepan Shabalin, Mateusz Piotrowski
abstract: MLP neurons in transformer language models are widely understood to be polysemantic, motivating transcoders - sparse, learned approximations of MLP layers - as interpretable replacement models for mechanistic analysis. However, recent work shows that MLP neurons can be used to recover sparse, interpretable circuits (Arora et al. 2026, Ye et al. 2025), raising the question of whether transcoders are necessary for circuit analysis. title: How Well Can LLMs Verbalize Mathematical Formulas? A Multi-Domain Evaluation
authors: Peter Volbach, Tim Schlippe
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong capabilities across natural language tasks. But their ability to generate accurate written verbalizations of mathematical formulas has not been systematically evaluated. Such verbalization is important for text-to-speech systems supporting audio-based learning and visually impaired users. title: MisleadQA: Diagnosing LLM Failures under Misleading Context
authors: Hui Wang, Bohao Chu, Qianli Wang et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used to answer questions from retrieved or user-provided context. However, provided context can be factually true yet out-of-scope, describing a different entity, time, or location from the one the question targets, and still lead models to a wrong answer. Prior work has mainly studied factually false or irrelevant context. title: CADS: Measuring the Incremental Contribution of LLM Proposers in Sequential Biological Screens
authors: Guanxing Chen, Nihui Shao, Haohuai He et al.
abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to guide sequential biological screens, yet standard evaluations rely on raw hit counts that conflate a proposer's value with the discovery capacity of the underlying algorithmic harness. Adaptive sampling and corrupted experimental readouts also leave standard feedback comparisons without a false-discovery guarantee. title: WAQS: Weight Absorption for Quadratic Probing and Affine Steering
authors: Ding Zhu, Mohammad Mahdi Khalili
abstract: Activation steering provides a lightweight alternative to fine-tuning for controlling large language model behavior. Existing methods, however, often face a trade-off between efficiency and expressiveness: fixed steering vectors incur negligible inference overhead but cannot adapt to the current model input, whereas input-dependent nonlinear interventions provide greater flexibility at additional runtime cost. title: FlashMap: Flow Map Speculative Decoding
authors: Jeff Shen, Zhejian Zhou, Ryan Lee et al.
abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model (LLM) inference by using a lightweight drafter to propose a block of tokens that the target model verifies in one parallel pass. Autoregressive drafters generate this block one token at a time, whereas block diffusion drafters such as DFlash generate it in one pass, making drafting faster. title: What Matters for NVFP4 Training? A Comparative Study of Low-Precision Pretraining Recipes
authors: Anjulie Agrusa, Andrei Panferov, Elizabeth Wei et al.
abstract: Training large language models directly in 4-bit floating-point (FP) formats promises substantial improvements in throughput and energy efficiency. While some recipe design choices have been validated at scale, many promising approaches remain untested beyond small models and short token horizons, leaving open the question of which trends will hold. title: fxBench: Evaluating and Understanding Formula Suggestions in Spreadsheets
authors: Sanket Mhatre, Sumit Gulwani, Vu Le et al.
abstract: Spreadsheets are among the most widely used tools for computations, and formulas are their core building blocks. Besides agentic spreadsheet tools, proactive formula suggestions enable significant productivity gains and are now available in popular spreadsheet software (Microsoft Excel and Google Sheets). title: PV-Decoding: Progressive Verification Decoding with Decode Gating for Diffusion Language Models
authors: Renxi Liu, Yiming Li, Shengyin Sun et al.
abstract: Discrete diffusion language models (dLLMs) offer an attractive alternative to autoregressive generation by updating multiple tokens in parallel, but their inference efficiency is still limited by the cost of safely committing tentative predictions. title: Write Once, Query Many: Evolving Compact Reusable Memory for Long Videos
authors: Kerui Chen, Jinglu Wang, Yun Wang et al.
abstract: Long videos often exceed the context capacity of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), while agentic search repeats costly video processing and grounding for each query. Reusable memory can amortize this cost, but must preserve information for questions unknown during construction. We propose Video-EMem, an evolvable video memory harness built on time-anchored perceptual observations. title: Which Long Documents Matter? A Controlled Study of Data Selection for Context Extension
authors: Junlong Jia, Jiang Zhou, Xing Wu et al.
abstract: Natural long documents are widely used for context extension, but which selection pipelines are effective remains unclear. We conduct a controlled comparison on Qwen2.5-3B at 128K under matched 6B-token continued-training budgets. Random sampling of natural long documents (random-long) outperforms repacking at longer evaluation lengths. title: Long Listening Thoughts: Eliciting Open Auditory Reasoning with Deliberative Perception and Cognitive Refinement
authors: Jaeyeon Kim, Chao-Han Huck Yang, Luoyi Zhang et al.
abstract: We introduce Long Listening Thoughts (LLT), a framework for constructing post-training datasets that improves audio reasoning by pairing deliberate perceptual grounding with explicit cognitive behaviors. On audio understanding and reasoning benchmarks, large audio-language models (LALMs) are limited primarily by perceptual errors, yet existing post-training datasets rely on audio descriptions of limited diversity. title: Blackbox Performance Analysis of LLM-based Network Control
authors: Mahdi Alizadeh, Pooria Namyar, Arvin Ghavidel et al.
abstract: LLMs are becoming an indispensable part of network control systems due to their impressive reasoning. Before such LLM-enabled systems can be deployed, it is imperative to develop tools that can audit their performance on previously unseen inputs. However, auditing these systems is challenging due to the inherent opacity of LLMs. LENS is the first step towards black-box performance analysis of LLM-enabled network control systems. title: GRaSP: Latency-Aware Optimization for Geo-Distributed Retrieval-Augmented Generation
authors: Hardik Ruparel, Raj Kumar Pandey, Pramod Kumar
abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is increasingly served across geo-distributed cloud and edge infrastructures, where wide-area latency, cross-region egress cost, and data-residency rules compete with retrieval quality. Conventional pipelines rank by semantic similarity alone and ignore where content lives, inflating tail latency and cost. title: Aptamers as a sandbox for lab-in-the-loop agentic molecular discovery
authors: Zachary Cutts, John Coller, Rachel Chen et al.
abstract: Despite breakthroughs in AI-driven molecular generation, existing discovery pipelines operate largely in silico, with wet-lab feedback reserved for validation rather than iterative improvement. Whether large language model (LLM)-based reasoning agents can accelerate de novo discovery by iterating with lab data remains unproven. title: AtomSD: Procedural Atom-Guided Self-Distillation for LLM Agents
authors: Bohan Yu, Pengfei Cao, Kai Tian et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) possess broad factual knowledge and strong reasoning capabilities, but solving complex tasks also requires procedural knowledge about how to act. Existing approaches often represent procedural knowledge through trajectories or bundled skills, limiting flexible reuse across interaction histories. This paper introduces Procedural Atoms, fine-grained and independently applicable units that represent Intent, When, Do, and Avoid guidance. Building on this representation,

title: MedPAO-Assist: Edge-Deployable, Modality-Aware Agentic AI for Radiology Report Structuring
authors: Shrish Shrinath Vaidya, Minmini Selvam, Ganapathy Krishnamurthi
abstract: The adoption of Large Language Models for radiology report structuring has been largely dominated by either proprietary cloud-based models or large open models requiring high-end GPUs for deployment, which is a critical bottleneck for clinical adoption in radiology workflows that demand data privacy and offline operation. title: Parametric Session States Recover Retrieval Intent without Replaying History
authors: Qingsen Ma, Dianyun Wang, Jiahong Liu et al.
abstract: Long-running assistants often interpret follow-up requests whose referents, constraints, and active goals were established many turns earlier. The central challenge is therefore not only context length, but retrieval intent: a current query such as ``use the previous configuration'' may omit the project, entity, and version terms needed to locate relevant evidence. title: Enhancing RAG-based Medical VQA with Gated Multimodal Representations
authors: Daniela Jimenez-Pano, Hugo Jair Escalante, Delia Irazú Hernández-Farías
abstract: Medical Vision-Language Models (Med-LVLMs) have shown strong performance in Medical Visual Question Answering (MVQA), yet they may still produce factually inconsistent responses. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) can mitigate this issue by incorporating external clinical evidence; however, retrieval is often guided by a single modality, potentially overlooking the joint semantics of medical images and clinical questions. title: Characterising and Analysing Retrieval-Augmented Generation Techniques
authors: Emmanuel Igbekele, Olawande Daramola
abstract: The advent of Large Language Models (LLMs) across many application domains has increased the need for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to reduce hallucinations and improve LLM performance. Thus far, several RAG techniques with impressive features and capabilities have been proposed in the literature, making it a herculean task to select the most appropriate RAG techniques for specific problem scenarios. title: On the Position Bias of Large Language Models: A Comprehensive Study
authors: Yining Li, Huayang Li, Lemao Liu et al.
abstract: Recent studies have shown that position bias remains a critical vulnerability in large language models (LLMs), undermining both the integrity of multiple-choice evaluations and the reliability of retrieval-augmented generation. However, existing understanding of this phenomenon is largely derived from studies with limited model coverage and English-centric benchmarks, leaving the behavior of frontier models and diverse languages underexplored. title: AI-Driven Reproducibility and Analytical Robustness in Scientific Discovery
authors: Shicheng Liu, Krista Opsahl-Ong, Andrew Drozdov et al.
abstract: Reproducible and analytically robust research findings are essential to scientific progress, but evaluating these properties typically requires costly manual effort. We investigate whether LLM agents can help automate reproduction and robustness analysis, using a medical case study grounded in the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) database, a widely used U.S. cancer registry underlying tens of thousands of published studies. title: DLite: History-free Speculative Decoding for Agentic AI
authors: Jiaming Xu, Hanzhen Wang, Tianlang Zhao et al.
abstract: Speculative decoding has become a mainstream technique for accelerating large language model (LLM) inference by using a lightweight draft model to generate candidate tokens that are subsequently verified by the target model. However, agentic workloads introduce long and continuously evolving contexts and frequent multi-turn interactions. title: On the possibilities and limitations of LLM-based multi-agent systems for multi-criteria decision-making in healthcare operations management
authors: Marco Boresta, Tommaso Giovannelli, Sepehr Namirad et al.
abstract: Multi-criteria models for healthcare operations need weights that express how stakeholders trade off patient waiting time, provider workload, and operating cost, but these weights are difficult to quantify. Teams of large language model (LLM) agents, each prompted to represent a stakeholder, have been used to supply them. title: From Trajectories to Differentiated Skills: Cognitive Differentiation for Self-Improving Agents
authors: Yewei Zhao, Derong Xu, Wei Chen et al.
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents tackle complex tasks through reasoning and interaction with external environments. Agent skills provide persistent, transferable capabilities that guide task planning, inform contextual decisions, support tool use, and enable executable procedures. title: RL-Guided Temporal Localization for Dual-Channel Retrieval in Long-Horizon Agent Memory
authors: Dabin Sheng, Zhe Wu, Jinming Zhao et al.
abstract: Time-aware retrieval is crucial for long-horizon LLM agents to effectively leverage ever-growing long-term memory. Existing methods focus on lexical or semantic similarity, leading to target memories being crowded out by temporally mismatched yet semantically similar candidates. title: Darwin-Claw: Environment-Adaptive Experience Consolidation for Recursively Self-Evolving Agents
authors: Mingze Yin, Xiaohan Wang, Dian Li et al.
abstract: While Large Language Model (LLM) agents have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across complex tasks, they predominantly operate in isolated sessions, lacking the ability to continually learn from historical interactions or adapt to user-specific environments. Existing self-evolution paradigms often indiscriminately inject raw interaction trajectories into memory or skill modules, leading to obscured behavioral patterns and compromised update controllability. title: SkillBrowser: Selective Skill Exposure for Scalable Skill-Using Agents
authors: Jin Ye, Yifan Jiang, Lan-zhe Guo
abstract: Large language model agents increasingly rely on skills to extend their capabilities in complex tasks. However, scalable skill use requires Selective Skill Exposure (SSE): providing relevant procedural content when needed while avoiding unnecessary exposure that may disrupt reasoning. Existing paradigms fall short in complementary ways. title: Robust Function Calling for LLM Agents Under Interface Drift
authors: Aniruddha Chattopadhyay, Kanishka Halder, Partha Sarathi Roy
abstract: Tool-augmented language-model agents rely on interface text: tool descriptions, argument schemas, and the candidate tool list shown at inference time. These interfaces often change after deployment even when the underlying tool semantics remain fixed, creating a practical reliability problem for function-calling systems. title: AgentOnto: Ontology-Guided LLM Agents for Enterprise Data Analytics
authors: Dayan Pan, Bincheng Zuo, Xiaojian Wang et al.
abstract: Enterprise data analysis requires agents to connect analytical requests with knowledge distributed across databases, business documents, and existing example tasks. Without an explicit representation of this knowledge, an agent may produce incorrect analytical results and cannot reliably incorporate feedback. title: MobileInject: Evaluating Reasoning-to-Action Security of MLLM-Based Mobile Agents under Cross-Modal Consistency Injection
authors: Songping Wang, Peiyang Li, Yi Huang et al.
abstract: Multimodal large language model (MLLM)-based mobile agents are rapidly evolving from conversational assistants into autonomous systems that perceive, reason over, and act on smartphone environments. This capability also exposes a new security risk: adversaries can embed malicious objectives in cross-application mobile content and steer agent behavior through indirect multimodal injection. title: Annotrace: A Workbench for Step-Level Annotation of Agent Traces
authors: Arun Josephraj Arokiaraj, Chenyi Huang, Sahan Bulathwela et al.
abstract: Every study of why LLM agents fail begins by labelling traces by hand, and every such study builds its own throwaway tool. Observability platforms record agent traces but offer no structured labelling; annotation tools label text but have no notion of a step, a delegation or a tool call, leaving it unclear what the smallest unit of execution to label should be. title: Beyond Marginal Influence: Interaction-Aware Memory Selection for LLM Agents
authors: BHVSP Subrahmanyam, Neeraj Choudhary
abstract: LLM-agent memory selection often uses retrieval rankings based on record relevance or individual influence. Such rankings cannot identify sufficient subsets under redundant or jointly necessary evidence. We study per-decision memory sufficiency: selecting a small subset that preserves full-memory behavior. title: MAS-Bai: Linguistically Informed Adaptive Multi-Agent Translation for Bowen-Script Bai
authors: Jingting Zheng, Hong Ren, Yuehan Cui et al.
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) remain unreliable for extremely low-resource languages whose writing systems conflict with high-resource pretraining priors. We study Bai-Chinese translation in the Bowen script, where Chinese characters are frequently borrowed phonetically rather than semantically, causing severe literal-translation hallucinations. title: Tree-Aware Posterior Distillation for Long-Horizon Agentic Reinforcement Learning
authors: Heming Zou, Qi Wang, Yixiu Mao et al.
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards has become a scalable post-training paradigm for large language models. However, training agents over long-horizon interactions presents two challenges: using only terminal rewards makes turn-level credit assignment sparse and high-variance, while sequential mini-batch updates on a fixed rollout batch introduce policy staleness as the current policy drifts from the behavior policy. title: Disentangling Language Effects on Tool Admission and Post-Retrieval Safety
authors: Aditya Nawal, Manit Baser, Mohan Gurusamy
abstract: LLM agents increasingly use retrieval tools across languages, yet their safety evaluation remains English-centric. It remains unclear whether language affects tool admission, post-retrieval generation, or both. title: Before Retrieval Begins: Safety and Tool-Use Decisions in LLM Agents
authors: Aditya Nawal, Manit Baser, Mohan Gurusamy
abstract: Large language models increasingly act as agents that call external tools, yet most tool-safety research examines only what follows a tool call. The prior decision of whether to call the tool remains largely unexamined and can influence downstream safety. Across the seven open-weight models, the unweighted model-average harm rate after admitted harmful requests is 74.5%. title: ParetoChat: An LLM-Based Interface for Interactive Multi-Objective Optimization
authors: Gokhan Ceyhan
abstract: Multi-objective optimization models are often deployed in settings where decision makers (DMs) must balance some conflicting criteria. In practice, however, stakeholders must translate their qualitative preferences between different criteria into numerical weights, priorities, or reference points required by optimization methods, which can be difficult to specify and interpret. title: Agentic In-Context Learning: What Algorithms Can Transformers Learn in Closed-Loop Interaction?
authors: Shiguang Wu, Yaqing Wang, Quanming Yao
abstract: The learning algorithm view of in-context learning (ICL) studies how fixed-parameter Transformers learn from supplied examples. Language model agents extend this setting through interaction: their actions determine what evidence enters context next. We call this regime Agentic In-Context Learning (Agentic ICL). title: Self-Evolving Agents Can Repair Failures but Struggle to Generalize from Them
authors: Weixiang Zhao, Yichen Zhang, Yanyan Zhao et al.
abstract: Experience-driven self-evolution offers a promising path for large language model (LLM) agents to continually improve through interaction. Yet existing approaches often rely on successful trajectories or external evaluation signals, leaving unclear whether agents can evolve when such positive anchors are unavailable. title: KiranaBench: Can a Language Model Run a Neighbourhood Shop?
authors: Bhuvan Arora, Ankita Karmakar, Chaitanya Jain et al.
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly evaluated on long-horizon tasks, including autonomously running a business. Existing benchmarks for this setting are almost exclusively English-language, Western in retail context, and single-agent, with the agent observing the business directly. We study how these results transfer to a multi-agent Indic setting. title: SAFE-Mem: Secure Agentic Memory with Fine-Grained Authority and Governance-Aware Retrieval
authors: Haoming Li, Dingyi Kang, Xu Hu et al.
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on persistent memory to support long-term reasoning and personalized interactions. However, information collected from external sources can introduce security risks when untrusted claims (i.e., atomic statements) are later treated as authorized preferences, policies, or permissions. title: Cooperation Without Adaptation: LLM Agents in a Collective-Risk Dilemma
authors: Trung-Kiet Huynh, Dao-Sy Duy-Minh, Chi-Nguyen Tran et al.
abstract: Language-model agents are increasingly deployed to act on behalf of people in settings where individual decisions shape shared outcomes. We examine whether five production models adapt their contributions to changing risks and partner behaviour, or instead follow a relatively fixed strategy. title: MS-Eval: Benchmarking Sub-Agent Delegation and Orchestration in MCP-Intensive Working Scenarios
authors: Bowen Ding, Qixin Wang, Lexing Ruan et al.
abstract: LLM agents are increasingly integrated into real-world works, yet they must handle diverse domain-specific tools and complex multi-sub-task problems that sequential tool invocation resolves inefficiently and with severe context bloat. The Main-Agent Delegation and Sub-Agent Execution (MAD-SAE) paradigm addresses these issues by delegating sub-tasks to specialized sub-agents for parallel execution in isolated contexts, but its delegation and orchestration quality remains unquantified. title: Self-Evolving Coding Agents via Harness-Policy Optimization
authors: Zhepei Wei, Wenlin Yao, Baolin Peng et al.
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents have shown promising potential in coding tasks, and their performance is jointly determined by the policy model and the harness that mediates their interaction with the environment. title: When Can You Trust an Agent's Own Verifier? Stress-Testing Counterfactual Rationale Verification Under Search Pressure and Oracle Access
authors: Jonghyun Lee, Moonsu Kim, Sunghwan Park
abstract: Automated agent design increasingly trusts a single score to decide whether a change is an improvement -- but a score optimized aggressively enough ceases to measure what it was meant to. When an agent also explains its design, that explanation is a second signal we can check without human labels: negate each stated claim, re-run, and observe whether performance drops. title: GatewayBench: Unified Capability and Security Evaluation Platform for MCP Gateways
authors: Yitian Zheng, Zhaorun Chen, Haoyu Li et al.
abstract: AI agents have increasingly interacted with external environments by invoking tools, with Model Context Protocol (MCP) emerging as a standard interface for connecting agents to heterogeneous tools and services. As organizations deploy agents at scale, MCP gateways have become a critical middleware layer for aggregating, governing, and shaping the tool surface exposed to agents. title: Beyond Large Language Models: A Mental World Model Framework for Mental Modeling, Simulation, Evolution, and Interpretability
authors: Qingshi Wang
abstract: Understanding and simulating how subjective cognition and mental states emerge, evolve, and shape behavior is essential for advancing artificial intelligence toward deeper social cognition and general intelligence. Existing large language models (LLMs) and Theory of Mind (ToM) methods primarily infer mental states from linguistic information, lacking unified mechanisms for subjective world construction, cognitive-psychological interactions, dynamic evolution, and historical dependencies. title: OwlSight: A Panoramic Monitor for Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
authors: Lewen Yan, Yanxu Zhu, Jie Zhang et al.
abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) monitoring offers actionable evidence for oversight AI systems, with the potential to enable early detection and intervention. However, existing approaches are focused on specific tasks, whereas the regulation of AI, particularly reasoning models, requires monitoring a broader range of tasks. title: Trapped in Your Story: Evaluating Narrative-Induced Sycophancy in Large Language Models
authors: Runtai Yang, Dandan Zhu, Kaiwei Zhang et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are known to exhibit sycophancy by adjusting their responses toward users' expressed views. However, real users often justify their opinions through reasons, personal experiences, causal explanations, and broader narratives, raising the question of whether such narratives can further steer model judgments. title: Perceive, Solve, Reason: Progressive Capability Formation in Time Series-LLMs
authors: Xin Qiu, Junlong Tong, Wei Zhang et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can now perceive, describe, and reason about images and audio, yet time series understanding remains underestimated: most work uses LLMs as forecasters and classifiers, reasoning studies are few and narrow, and no suite trains and evaluates the full range of capabilities. title: S-GAP: Stealthy Graph Attack Primitives for Graph Large Language Models
authors: Wenda Li, Tongya Zheng, Shunyu Liu et al.
abstract: Graph Large Language Models (GraphLLMs) enable powerful semantic understanding and reasoning over Text-Attributed Graphs (TAGs), while their semantic reasoning may exhibit vulnerabilities to perturbations in node text and graph structure under adversarial attack evaluation. title: On the Tip of the Tongue: First-Token Cueing as a Behavioral Probe of Recall Failures in LLMs
authors: Jaewon Sok, Jewon Yeom, Seonghyeon Park et al.
abstract: Large language models often answer factual questions incorrectly in closed-book settings, and such errors are usually attributed to missing knowledge. Yet models often encode answers they fail to produce. We show that many closed-book errors are first-token recall failures: the model commits to a wrong first token, but once given the right one it completes the answer and often recognizes it as correct. title: Self-Reflective Chain-of-Thought (SRCoT): Evidence-Based Text Generation via a Closed-Loop Retrieve--Reflect--Revise Pipeline on Edge LLMs
authors: Fabian Broszio, Michael Hoffmann, Adrian Paschke
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate fluent outputs that lack source support or conflict with local operational constraints. We introduce Self-Reflective Chain-of-Thought (SRCoT), a modular architecture that organizes generation as a closed Retrieve--Reflect--Revise loop. SRCoT separates environment state, persistent knowledge, accumulated experience, and short-term memory into provenance-labeled stores. title: Verbalising Model's Computation for Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness Detection
authors: Yujing Wang, Yulan He, Wenya Wang et al.
abstract: Current Chain-of-Thought (CoT) verification methods detect reasoning faithfulness from model outputs or static activations, but are limited in explaining how unfaithfulness develops during generation. We introduce VERITAS to verbalise the model's computation: how different reasoning anchors emerge, transfer across layers, and surface in the output. authors: Uriel Dolev, Idan Schwartz, Yoav Goldberg
abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) controllability, the ability of reasoning models to control properties of their CoT, is consequential for both their usefulness and reliable oversight. Recent work evaluates this capability by measuring whether models follow CoT constraints given in the user prompt, and reports very low controllability across models. title: Who Pays for Efficient Inference? Confidence-Based Small-to-Large LLM Routing Across Tasks and Languages
authors: Md Sabbir Hossen, Anichur Rahman, Pabon Shaha et al.
abstract: Small-to-large language model routing can reduce inference cost by escalating difficult inputs while retaining easier ones on a smaller model. Its success, however, depends on identifying examples that benefit from escalation, and the reliability of confidence across multilingual tasks remains unclear. title: Not All Test-Time Compute Is Evidence: Model-Specific Bias in LLM Reasoning
authors: Ming Shen, Tianjun Yao
abstract: Test-time scaling methods implicitly assume that additional computation from the same model provides independent evidence. We show that this assumption fails within a single reasoning model: errors are correlated across repeated samples, across reasoning depth, and in the model's own self-evaluation, so more compute from the same model is not more evidence. title: Prism Attention: Proposal-Refined Index Sharing Mechanism for Efficient LLMs Inference
authors: Zhenxu Tian, Kebin Liu, Zhengwu Yang et al.
abstract: Long-context decoding in large language models (LLMs) is increasingly bottlenecked by the memory and computation required to attend over an ever-growing Key-Value (KV) cache at each autoregressive step. authors: Yinlong Xu, Jianfeng Huang, Zhengdong Zhou et al.
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable success in complex reasoning through explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT), but the associated computational overhead and token verbosity remain significant barriers to efficiency. authors: Jize Jiang, Chengxiang Zhai
abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have brought impressive performance across diverse tasks; however, shortcomings remain in logical reasoning, including inconsistencies under linguistic variation. authors: Lijia Liu, Kyohei Atarashi, Jiyi Li et al.
abstract: Formulating optimization problems from raw inputs of problem descriptions and data is time-consuming and costly. While Large Language Models (LLMs) offer a promising way to automate this process, existing benchmarks overestimate their capabilities by relying on idealized inputs where all data is relevant and complete. authors: Jianguo Huang, Zhiyi Lyu, Fuxiang Zhang et al.
abstract: Tree search enhances multi-step reasoning in large language models (LLMs), yet prevailing methods expand every step with a fixed budget, irrespective of the marginal utility of expansion. title: The Reliance Hypothesis: Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness Rises as Language Resource Level Falls
authors: Lucas Resck, Jingyi Sun, Qianli Wang et al.
abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) faithfulness matters for monitoring, explaining and safely deploying large language models, yet it has been studied mostly in English. Languages differ in level, the amount of text available to learn from, so models know less in lower-resource languages, which may change how much they rely on their reasoning. title: HydraLLM: Adaptive Width Slicing for Elastic Text and Vision-Language Models
authors: Oscar Kemme, Janek Haberer, Ali Hojjat et al.
abstract: LLMs and LVLMs are increasingly deployed across heterogeneous hardware, ranging from data-center GPUs to resource-constrained edge devices. Their fixed-size architectures limit the ability to reuse a single model across deployment settings with different compute, latency, and model-size targets. We introduce HydraLLM, an elastic MQA-based architecture. title: CoTA++: Understanding the Repeat Curse in dMLLMs from an Information Flow Perspective
authors: Qiyan Zhao, Xiaofeng Zhang, Xu-Yao Zhang et al.
abstract: Diffusion-based multimodal large language models (dMLLMs) decode by iterative denoising with bidirectional attention, which precludes the standard autoregressive key--value cache. Practical deployments therefore rely on approximate caching that reuses intermediate states across denoising steps. title: Causal Value Attribution of Marketing Labels in LLM-Generated Ads: A Deconfounder Approach
authors: Danhong You, Wei Jiang,  Zhiqiang et al.
abstract: As AI-generated content becomes commoditized, economic value increasingly shifts from final artifacts to the upstream expertise used to specify inputs that steer LLM generation. Yet organizations lack methods for valuing this expertise and identifying which individual skills or configurations causally improve performance. title: COMET: Decoupled Distillation, Routing, and Capacity Control for Task-Agnostic Continual Vision--Language Learning
authors: Seungyoon Woo, Keonhee Park, Gunhee Kim
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) such as CLIP retain zero-shot recognition ability, but their open-world use often requires task-agnostic continual learning: tasks arrive sequentially, past data are unavailable, task identity is unknown, and the backbone cannot be retrained. title: FederatedBytes: Tokenizer-Free, Byte-Level Small Language Models for Efficient Multimodal Federated Learning
authors: Ali Sarabadani, Massimo Piccardi, Mehran Abolhasan et al.
abstract: Federated Learning (FL) is a powerful machine learning framework that allows building a global model from the contributions of multiple, distributed clients, while ensuring the privacy of their local data. However, its heavy computational and communication overheads challenge its use for contemporary AI workloads such as natural language processing (NLP) and multimodal analysis. authors: Ziyun Zou, Jiwoo Hong, Yifan Lu et al.
abstract: Multimodal preference alignment often follows a score-based RLHF pipeline: a reward model is first trained to learn human preferences, then used to score on-policy responses and optimize the response model's generation. title: VISTA: Steering LLMs with Latent User Values Inferred from a Few Survey Answers
authors: Yinuo Xu, Jadie Adams, Brian Hu et al.
abstract: Personalizing a language model requires knowing what a person values, which stays largely consistent across tasks. Yet most methods either learn task-specific preferences or place the user's profile in the prompt, where models struggle to act on it. authors: Ponhvoan Srey, Jason Lucas, Pittawat Taveekitworachai et al.
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) encode substantial factual knowledge. Yet, estimating confidence in factual claims reliably remains challenging. We study likelihood-based factual confidence from the complementary perspectives of discrimination and calibration across multilingual factual statements.
